rooms.name: The Sea Paintings
rooms.short: Surf, reef and open water, including three canvases eight feet wide.
rooms.quote: When the canvas is flat, my whole body becomes part of the brush.
essay: Chas Pulido paints with the canvas flat on the studio floor in San Francisco. He works it from all four sides, pouring and throwing acrylic from above, so each painting is made by moving around it as much as standing in front of it.

The Sea Paintings are nine works about the water, made over 2025 and 2026. Three of them are eight feet wide. Some are surf, some are reef and some are open water at night. The coast paintings carry the warmth of the land behind them.
Pulido came to painting without formal training and still talks about the work in plain terms. He wants it to feel joyful, and he trusts what happens when he stops steering the paint.
works: White breaks across a warm ground like surf hitting rock, thrown in long arcs over a tangle of dark blue.
A rust-colored sky over a dark sea, with white spray rising off the waterline. The companion to Crashing Coasts.
Bright blue water with white spray and flecks of pink and black, all leaning the same way like wind coming off the shore.
A blue field scattered with bright drops of color, above a dark reef packed with red and coral.
Long lines of red, yellow and white thrown across deep blue, crossing each other the way fireworks do over water.
The tallest canvas in the series. Layers of blue pushed into swirls, with gold flecks scattered through the middle.
Bright drips of every color running down a black ground, like fish lit up in a dark tank.
Six columns of orange, red and yellow rising out of cobalt blue, like kelp lit from below.
Red and yellow rays fan in from the top corners over a row of drips standing on sea-glass blue.

rooms.name: The Smile Paintings
rooms.short: Bouquets in red and pink, from a single bloom on sky blue to rows of three and four.
rooms.quote: Life is too short to make sad art.
essay: For two years Chas Pulido kept returning to the bouquet. A stem, a burst of color at the top, a ground underneath. He titles each one a smile.

The Smile Paintings bring seven of them together. Some hold a single bouquet the size of a person. Others line three or four up like a row of guests, each one thrown in the same gesture and each one landing differently.
The grounds change from painting to painting, from pale sky blue to warm desert brown to a deep night blue, and the red at the center holds the room together.
works: A single bouquet bursting in red and pink against pale sky blue, rising from a base of gold and orange.
Red and pink flames rising out of a band of gold over teal. The tallest bouquet in the room.
Three bouquets in red, orange and violet standing against a deep night blue.
Four pink and red bouquets in a row over grey water.
Three bouquets in red and violet over pale blue, with white flecks thrown across the lower half.
Three bouquets of long colored strands rising over a purple ground.
Three bouquets in red and pink on woven gold stems, over a ground of brown and gold.

rooms.name: The Forest Paintings
rooms.short: Single trees and whole groves, from a tree on a canvas three feet wide to a meadow at ground level.
rooms.quote: Some of the best pieces come from the moment you stop trying to control it and start responding to it.
essay: Each of the Forest Paintings starts from a trunk and opens into a crown of thrown color that fills the top of the canvas.
Four of the eight are single trees, hung tall the way you would look up at one. The rest open out into groves of birch and gold-trunked trees and finally into a meadow at ground level.
The grounds run hot and cool together. A tree can stand on burning red or on night blue, and the canopy above it carries every color in between.
works: A single tree with a crown of yellow and green, standing on a burning red ground.
One tree in orange and teal blossom, its trunk rising out of red.
The narrowest canvas in the room. A tall, thin tree threaded with red, white and green.
A slender gold trunk under a round blue crown, over a ground of lavender and sky blue.
A row of white birch trunks under a canopy of red, yellow and pink, against blue.
Three gold trunks under a dense red and blue canopy, set against swirling grey-blue.
A low band of orange and gold flowers along the bottom of a deep brown field.
A meadow of pink, yellow and violet blooms rising out of brown. The smallest work in the room.

rooms.name: The Flare Paintings
rooms.short: Six large bursts and eruptions on hot grounds of red, orange and violet.
rooms.quote: When the canvas is flat, my whole body becomes part of the brush.
essay: The Flare Paintings are the loudest work in the studio. Chas Pulido lays down a hot ground of red, orange or violet, then throws color across it hard enough that it lands as a burst.

Some flares travel sideways across the canvas. Others go straight up, in columns he calls geysers. Every painting here is at least five feet on its long side, three are six feet square, and Breathing Fire runs eight feet wide.
Hung as two walls, they read like a single day of light: the sideways flares from dawn violet to the red of midday, and across the room the geysers rising out of evening.
works: Blue and gold lines driven diagonally across eight feet of red.
Blue and white thrown in a single burst across a deep orange-red ground.
Red and gold strokes flung across soft violet, like light breaking through cloud.
A fountain of color bursting upward out of charcoal grey.
Three columns of yellow, blue and violet rising through a ground of rose and red.
Three dense columns of white, blue and violet erupting from bright orange.
